classification.difficultyReason: Students extend the preceding factorisation procedure to mixed products and reciprocal equations, retain all branches, reject impossible ratios and round quadrant solutions.

content.prompt: Solve for $\theta\in[0^{\circ},360^{\circ})$. Answer to the nearest minute where necessary.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}2\sin\theta\cos\theta-\sin\theta&=0\\\sin\theta(2\cos\theta-1)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\sin\theta=0$ or $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$.
For $\sin\theta=0$, $\theta=0^{\circ},180^{\circ}$.
For $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, the reference angle is $60^{\circ}$ and cosine is positive in Q1 and Q4, giving $\theta=60^{\circ},300^{\circ}$.
Thus $\theta=0^{\circ},60^{\circ},180^{\circ},300^{\circ}$. The upper endpoint $360^{\circ}$ is excluded.

$$\begin{align*}2\sin^2\theta+\sin\theta-1&=0\\(2\sin\theta-1)(\sin\theta+1)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$ or $\sin\theta=-1$.
For $\sin\theta=\tfrac12$, the reference angle is $30^{\circ}$ and sine is positive in Q1 and Q2, giving $\theta=30^{\circ},150^{\circ}$.
For $\sin\theta=-1$, $\theta=270^{\circ}$.
Thus $\theta=30^{\circ},150^{\circ},270^{\circ}$.

Since the denominators require $\cos\theta\ne0$, multiply by $\cos^2\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}1+2\cos\theta&=8\cos^2\theta\\8\cos^2\theta-2\cos\theta-1&=0\\(4\cos\theta+1)(2\cos\theta-1)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\cos\theta=-\tfrac14$ or $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$.
For $\cos\theta=-\tfrac14$, use the positive ratio:
$$A=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac14\right).$$
Cosine is negative in Q2 and Q3, so $\theta=180^{\circ}-A,180^{\circ}+A$, giving $104^{\circ}29',255^{\circ}31'$ to the nearest minute.
For $\cos\theta=\tfrac12$, $\theta=60^{\circ},300^{\circ}$.
Thus $\theta=60^{\circ},104^{\circ}29',255^{\circ}31',300^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}3\cos^2\theta+5\cos\theta-2&=0\\(3\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+2)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\cos\theta=\tfrac13$ or $\cos\theta=-2$. Reject $-2$ because $-1\le\cos\theta\le1$.
$$A=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac13\right).$$
Cosine is positive in Q1 and Q4, so $\theta=A,360^{\circ}-A$.
To the nearest minute, $\theta=70^{\circ}32',289^{\circ}28'$.

Since the denominators require $\sin\theta\ne0$, multiply by $\sin^2\theta$:
$$\begin{align*}4-4\sin\theta-15\sin^2\theta&=0\\15\sin^2\theta+4\sin\theta-4&=0\\(5\sin\theta-2)(3\sin\theta+2)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\sin\theta=\tfrac25$ or $\sin\theta=-\tfrac23$.
For $\sin\theta=\tfrac25$, let $A=\sin^{-1}(\tfrac25)$. Sine is positive in Q1 and Q2, so $\theta=A,180^{\circ}-A$, giving $23^{\circ}35',156^{\circ}25'$.
For $\sin\theta=-\tfrac23$, let $B=\sin^{-1}(\tfrac23)$. Sine is negative in Q3 and Q4, so $\theta=180^{\circ}+B,360^{\circ}-B$, giving $221^{\circ}49',318^{\circ}11'$.
All angles are rounded to the nearest minute.

$$\begin{align*}4\sin^3\theta-3\sin\theta&=0\\\sin\theta(4\sin^2\theta-3)&=0\end{align*}$$
Either $\sin\theta=0$ or $\sin^2\theta=\tfrac34$.
For $\sin\theta=0$, $\theta=0^{\circ},180^{\circ}$.
Otherwise $\sin\theta=\pm\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, with reference angle $60^{\circ}$. Positive sine gives $60^{\circ},120^{\circ}$; negative sine gives $240^{\circ},300^{\circ}$.
Thus $\theta=0^{\circ},60^{\circ},120^{\circ},180^{\circ},240^{\circ},300^{\circ}$. The upper endpoint $360^{\circ}$ is excluded.
